verdict: Avoid new textile-trading exposure in Delhi; lend only to asset-backed, cash-and-carry traders with clean GST and no speculative yarn inventory.
title: Delhi textile trading: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business actually is
**A Delhi textile trader buys yarn or fabric, holds it briefly, and sells into garment units and wholesale markets; cash is made on turnover and timing, not on price.** Value sits in inventory and receivables, so the working-capital cycle is the whole credit story. ICRA's fabric methodology flags inventory holding plus receivables as the two drivers of working capital, with weaving fixed-capital and working-capital intensive and funding needs typically high [8][9]. **So when a proposal lands, check the inventory-turn and receivable-days first; if either is longer than the customer's own past year, ask why before touching the limit.**

## What has changed now
**Delhi is running behind the country: GST collections +2.7% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1%, and electricity demand +6.5% versus India +9.5% [D].** Both are local stress signals, and the data pack's own call is AVOID at score 12 [D]. Nationally, bank credit is +29.1% YoY against activity +6.1%, a +23.0 pp gap, with repo at 5.5% and a tightening stance [D] — money is chasing borrowers faster than trade is growing. **Local reporting says North India cotton yarn prices are stable but liquidity is tight in Delhi and Ludhiana, with weak demand and payment constraints [3]; treat stable prices with tight liquidity as a warning, not comfort.** A fire at a Mangolpuri garment factory [2] is a reminder that uninsured stock and premises risk sit inside this trade. Peer results are mixed and mostly not Delhi: KPR revenue +18.9% YoY with 25.7% EBITDA margin [5], Raymond Lifestyle income +5% YoY at 14.4% margin [7], Vishal Fabrics' export order story is from December 2025 and dated [6]. Vardhman's MD expects a 3-4% cotton gap for one to two years and notes New York futures moved from about $0.67-0.68 to about $0.80 [4] — that is the US market, in USD per pound. **Sources say little about Delhi specifically, so lean on first principles and these peers.**

## Where to grow
**Pursue traders who sell against confirmed garment-unit orders, carry fast-moving fabric, and show GST turnover matching bank credits.** Prefer borrowers with owned or leased godown security and a second-generation trade record. **Avoid traders holding speculative yarn stock, those with receivables beyond collect-from-customer days, and anyone whose sales are concentrated in one buyer.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure as cash credit against stock and receivables with a 25% margin, monthly stock statements, and a drawing power recalculated each month.** Take GST returns monthly, bank statements monthly, and stock-and-receivable ageing every quarter. **If drawing power utilisation stays above 90% for two months, cut the limit and ask for receivables ageing.**

## Early-warning signs
- **GST turnover falling below bank credits for two quarters (quarterly) -> freeze enhancement and inspect godown.**
- **Receivable days stretching beyond the customer's own prior year (monthly) -> demand ageing and stop fresh bills discounting.**
- **Inventory ageing past collect-from-customer days (monthly) -> revalue stock and reduce drawing power.**
- **Cheque returns or delayed interest (monthly) -> move to secured, fully drawn term loan only.**
watch: GST turnover below credits for two quarters -> freeze limit enhancement and inspect stock
Utilisation above 90% for two months -> cut limit and demand receivables ageing
Days beyond customer's prior year -> stop bill discounting and seek collection plan
Any return or delay -> convert to secured term loan, no fresh cash credit
